text: Red-teaming exists to find jailbreaks before real users do. This lesson is conceptual and defensive — what a jailbreak is, and why these techniques can work at all. It's not a working recipe for breaking any specific model.

A jailbreak is an input crafted to get a model to produce an output its safety training was meant to prevent. The request is functionally the same thing refusal training would normally catch — it's just framed so it doesn't look, to the model, like what that training learned to recognize.

That's possible because of a distributional gap. Safety training covers a large but finite sample of phrasings, while the space of all possible inputs is effectively unbounded and can't be fully enumerated by any training process. The model's trained refusal behavior is reliable close to what it saw in training, and that reliability degrades, in ways that are hard to fully predict, as a request drifts further from that distribution while still functionally asking for the same thing.

Research and red-teaming have documented a few recurring categories, described here only conceptually. Roleplay or persona framing wraps a request in fiction or simulation. Obfuscation and encoding keep the intent but change the surface form away from what training saw. And many-shot context stuffing uses a long run of examples to shift the model's behavior pattern before the real request even appears, exploiting the fact that everything already in context shapes behavior, not just the final line.

Each documented pattern gets patched once it's found — that's the red-teaming loop from last lesson — but patching a known pattern narrows one instance of the gap, it doesn't close the gap itself. Next lesson: refusal training, the defense all of this is trying to get around, and its own limits.
